Headteacher's Welcome
Haggerston School is a high-performing, vibrant academy that sits at the heart of the Community Schools Trust (CST). We are unapologetically ambitious for every student and believe in the power of education to transform lives.
Our school culture - The Haggerston Way - is built on the pillars of Aspiration, Creativity and Character. These values guide everything we do. We set high expectations, promote intellectual curiosity and resilience, and foster a strong sense of personal and collective responsibility.
Academic success is central to our mission. We deliver a challenging, knowledge-rich curriculum that prepares students not just for exams, but for the demands of adult life. Our outcomes reflect our commitment to rigour and excellent teaching. But we also believe that education should build confidence, compassion, and the ability to think independently.
We want school to be a place of possibility. Whether in the classroom, through the Arts, on the sports field or in leadership roles, students at Haggerston are encouraged to discover their strengths and push themselves to improve every day.
I hope this prospectus offers you a glimpse into the culture, energy and ambition that define our school. We value the diversity of our students and are committed to helping every child realise their aspirations.
It is a privilege to lead this exceptional community. I warmly invite you to visit, meet our staff and students, and experience the Haggerston Way for yourself.
Saad Anjum, Headteacher

School Vision / Ethos
The Haggerston Way: Our Values
Our Mission Statement is expressed through three key value statements that shape everything we do at Haggerston School.
Aspiration - We strive to be the best version of ourselves.
Aspiration means working with purpose. It’s not just wanting success — it’s earning it through effort, focus, and resilience. We teach students that aspirations are goals with a plan, built on knowledge, attendance, and hard work. At Haggerston, aspiration is effort with direction.
Creativity - We create beautiful work to inspire others.
Beautiful work is thoughtful, precise, and knowledge-rich — whether it’s writing, design, or problem-solving. Creativity and knowledge go hand in hand: curiosity and imagination are nurtured through growing understanding, skill, and discipline. At Haggerston, creativity is rigour in action.
Character - We are articulate, confident and determined individuals.
Character is not inherited — it’s built. Through daily habits and modelling, we teach resilience, respect, and integrity. With strong character, our students lead with confidence, face challenges, and contribute positively to their communities. At Haggerston, character is taught, not assumed.

pageCache.text:
Literacy Vision
Why literacy matters
Reading ability shapes a child’s experience of school more than almost anything else. When pupils can move confidently through a text, follow an explanation and unpack complex ideas, they learn more and feel more successful. The EEF’s Literacy Guidance Report highlights this link clearly: stronger reading leads to stronger attainment across subjects.
Knowing our starting points
Every Year 7 pupil completes a baseline reading assessment so we have an accurate picture from the outset. This prevents gaps from being missed and gives teachers the information they need to pitch lessons appropriately. The approach mirrors the EEF’s guidance on the importance of diagnostic assessment
What literacy looks like in daily practice
These routines help pupils internalise the habits of confident readers and articulate thinkers.
Our ambition: every child reading at chronological age by Year 9
We want all pupils to reach their chronological reading age by the end of Year 9. That milestone ensures they enter Key Stage 4 ready to access challenging exam texts, instructions and extended writing without unnecessary barriers. OECD research shows that adolescent reading confidence remains a strong predictor of later educational and economic outcomes.
Targeted intervention where it is needed
When a pupil falls significantly behind, we act quickly. Interventions range from one-to-one phonics through Toe-by-Toe, to small-group reading programmes, to structured digital support through Lexia. Each option is matched to a pupil’s assessed need, and progress is reviewed through regular retesting. The principles are well established in the National Reading Panel’s evidence base
Literacy woven into our wider culture
Our Politeness Focus of the Week includes a Word of the Week, shared across assemblies, tutor time and line-ups. Staff use it in conversations and reward pupils who adopt it accurately. This reinforces both vocabulary growth and the calm, courteous culture we want pupils to experience every day.
Keeping an eye on impact
Attendance to interventions remains high, and retesting shows clear movement for many pupils. We monitor closely so that support doesn’t drift. The adjust-and-respond cycle we follow is consistent with the SEND Code of Practice’s graduated approach.
A reading culture that supports achievement
At Haggerston, literacy isn’t a separate strand. It is part of how we teach, how pupils communicate and how we open doors to future learning. When every child reaches their reading age by Year 9, they gain access to the full curriculum and the confidence to tackle what comes next.
That is the vision we are working towards - lesson by lesson, habit by habit.

Welcome to Haggerston Sixth Form
A Warm Welcome to Haggerston Sixth Form.
Haggerston Sixth Form is a vibrant community of talented and ambitious young people. Our focus is on academic excellence and developing leaders of the future. Our Sixth Form is in the top 25% nationally, for progress.
Our students benefit from high levels of exceptional teaching, small class sizes and individual support. Last year, all our students progressed on to university or degree level apprenticeships with a significant number (44%) securing places at Russell Group Universities, more than double the London average.
Our curriculum offer is built around academic, ‘facilitating’ subjects with a small number of vocational courses. The majority of students study three A- Levels, and the Extended Professional Qualification and we expect all our students to engage with a number of enrichment experiences alongside their academic courses. We work with The Access Project, who provide specialist, individual support with university applications, including bespoke societies for students who aspire to study medicine, law or to attend Oxford or Cambridge.
Situated in a Grade II listed, historic building, sixth formers at Haggerston benefit from fantastic, state of the art facilities. Our students enjoy a rich variety of experiences, from guest lectures and cultural visits to links with our business partners in the city. Our students feel part of a tight-knit community, where they can develop their individual talents and flourish into confident and successful young adults.
View our Sixth Form Prospectus here.
Mr S Anjum, Headteacher

History and Architecture
Haggerston School was designed (1962) and built (1964-67) by the celebrated modernist architect Ernö Goldfinger. The school is believed to have admitted its first students in January 1966 as Haggerston Girls’ Secondary School.
Over the years, the school became Haggerston Girls’ School and then Haggerston School in September 2009 when it became co-educational with its own sixth form. A major refurbishment under the Building Schools for the Future (BSF) programme was completed in 2012. This included remodelling of the main teaching block and construction of a new state-of -the-art, design, technology and art block, and increased the capacity of the school from 900 to 1,100. Haggerston School is now an Academy after joining The Community Schools Trust in September 2023.
Erno Goldfinger (1902-87) was born in Budapest, and lived in Vienna and Paris, where he studied architecture under Auguste Perret, one of the first architects to develop the use of reinforced concrete aesthetically. Perret’s buildings of the 1920s and 1930s are rigorously classical and expressive of their concrete structure, and this influence is clearly visible in Haggerston School. The elevations follow the Golden Section, a use of mathematical proportion that owes considerably to Perret’s inspiration. Goldfinger’s work is unique in Britain in combining the influences of Perret with detailing and plan-forms derived from Le Corbusier; he is also unique in having known both men personally.
Haggerston School is one of the outstanding school buildings of its period. It is Goldfinger’s only secondary school and is Grade II Listed.
The plan has three linked blocks, a central teaching spine incorporating first-floor library, with entrance block to west containing an assembly hall and staff accommodation, and gymnasia to east. It is built in a brutalist style using a vast amount of blockish brickwork, timber, glass and concrete. The floor slabs are expressed as continuous shallow bands with a bush-hammered texture, while the exposed columns are broad and smooth faced, High concrete parapets top all the blocks.
The school’s extensive modernisation and refurbishment between 2010-2012 was designed by Avanti Architects and included a brand new ‘creative’ block. It received a commendation from “The Hackney Design Awards 2012” and was officially reopened by Dame Kelly Holmes (double Olympic gold medallist) in 2012.

School Clubs
Every Friday afternoon, students have the opportunity to take part in a wide range of enrichment activities designed to help them discover new interests, develop skills and enjoy experiences beyond the classroom.
Every term, students can choose from an exciting programme of clubs and activities taking place across the school.
Our Enrichment Offer
Friday afternoons | 12:15pm – 1:30pm
Alongside our Friday enrichment programme, students can also access a range of clubs throughout the week at lunchtime and after school.
Why Enrichment Matters
Our enrichment programme gives students the opportunity to:
We want every student to have the opportunity to try something new and make the most of their time at Haggerston.
Explore new interests and discover new passions
Develop confidence and independence
Build valuable skills beyond the classroom
Meet new people and build friendships
Strengthen their sense of community and belonging
How Do Students Choose?
Students select their enrichment activity for each term using the invite sent to parents and carers via Evolve.
Places are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis, so we encourage students to make their choices promptly.
If a club is full, students can be placed on a waiting list. Places may become available during the term and will then be offered to students on the waiting list.
Attendance
We want students to make the most of their enrichment opportunities. If a student misses three sessions, their place may be reassigned to another student on the waiting list.

Our Curriculum
Mission Statement
The Haggerston Way: Our Mission Statement is expressed through three key value statements that shape everything we do at Haggerston School.
Curriculum Rationale
Our curriculum aims to deliver the following outcomes:
We provide a high-quality curriculum and ensure they capture the following principles:
For more information about our curriculum, please complete the enquiry form on the Contact Us page.
Points 2.1 to 2.4 below demonstrate how we work to achieve this:
2.1. Our curriculum sets out to achieve the following aims:
A. Allow students to identify core knowledge and skills to be learned, retained and recalled over time.
B. Carefully identify components of learning and sequence these across different years, which leads to students being able to access composite knowledge later on in their shared journey.
C. Have comprehensive mid-term plans (MTPs) that build on the LTPs.
D. Provide a truly personalised curriculum.
E. Support students with essential skills for memory recall. We help students develop a knowledge and understanding of the National Curriculum by:
F. Create independent learners who can self-regulate.
G. Develop ‘examination literacy’, application of knowledge, self-regulation, stamina and resilience amongst other important skills required to be successful in public exams.
H. Develop behaviour and attitudes reflective of responsible citizens, able to read, write and communicate well, to allow them to play a positive role in British life.
2.2. Students study the following National Curriculum subjects at Haggerston School:
We offer a broad and balanced curriculum. All of our students take GCSE English Language, GCSE English Literature, GCSE Maths and Core PE. Additionally, all of our students will complete GCSEs in either triple or combined Sciences.
We allow our students three option choices in their GCSEs.
The vast majority of our students will choose highly academic subjects which will qualify them to meet the standards required for the English Baccalaureate (EBacc), a measure that has been identified to ensure students are prepared for academic careers. We do not believe that this route is suitable for all our students. Some students will choose two options and they are given additional time to improve their literacy and/or numeracy skills which will help them to access the full curriculum.
We offer the following subjects as an additional GCSE option in year 9: History, Geography, Spanish, Business Studies, Computer Science, Art, Drama, Music, Sociology, PE, Product Design, Textiles and Food.
In year 11, we expect all our students to practise examination skills after school for selected subjects. This is a timely strategy to ensure students develop self-regulation, stamina and resilience among other essential skills required for their GCSEs and beyond.
2.3. How do we assess and report what our students learn?
Assessment exists to make learning visible so that teachers and leaders can act quickly, precisely and responsibly. Assessment is not undertaken to generate data for its own sake; rather, it informs teaching, identifies misconceptions and supports timely intervention. At Haggerston School, assessment is rooted in our curriculum and provides meaningful evidence of what pupils know, understand and can do.
Our assessment model is designed to maximise the quality of information while minimising unnecessary workload. Where appropriate, efficient assessment approaches, such as OMR marked multiple choice assessments and other digitally marked assessments, are used to provide reliable curriculum level analysis while reducing unnecessary teacher workload. AI supported marking may be used where appropriate and in line with CST guidance. All AI-generated marks remain subject to teacher moderation and quality assurance before informing reporting or intervention decisions.
Formative assessment
Summative assessments
Nationally standardised assessments
In-class teachers are responsible for formative verbal and written feedback
Dynamic Progress Reporting (DPR) will facilitate learning collaboration between students, teachers and parents and ensure students are learning against the expected standards
Assignments (formerly known as homework) are an essential component to learning whereby students revisit those topics that are not yet secure
Assignments are set through the DPR.
From September 2026:
• Years 7–10 complete two formal interim assessments.
• Years 11–13 complete three formal interim assessments.
The results from summative assessments will be used by teachers to inform DPR judgements
OMR assessments, KO tests, prelims and department assessments linked directly to the curriculum.
Granada Learning (GL) Pass Tests are undertaken by all year groups (Y7 - 10). These are nationally recognised, robust self-evaluation systems for the standardised measurement of pupil aptitudes
GL Progress Tests are nationally benchmarked Progress Tests for Maths, English and Science available for the Years 7, 8 and 9. They will be used to support our own verdict on student progress
NGRT Tests are reading assessments used to identify pupils whose reading age may limit access to the wider curriculum. Outcomes are used to plan targeted intervention and monitor progress over time
GCSE (or equivalent level 2) examinations
A-Level (or BTEC) Qualifications
Please see our summative assessment map
Our curriculum sets out a clear, differentiated learning journey for students with different starting points at KS2. For each subject and for each year group, we have carefully identified key learning objectives, which are carefully linked and sequenced to both KS3, KS4 and KS5 programmes of study.
Students are expected to demonstrate a ‘secured’ understanding in these key learning objectives within the course of a year
Teachers are encouraged to assess students’ learning every lesson through the deployment of various forms of AfL strategies. We also expect our teachers to ‘live mark’ students’ work during lessons. Teachers routinely use the CST Teaching and Learning Framework (Explicit Direct Instruction) to assess understanding through strategies such as memory retrieval, Turn and Talk, Mini Whiteboards, explicit vocabulary instruction, live marking and Show Call.
As part of our CST teaching and learning framework, teachers are encouraged to use the DPR when appropriate, as a live tool for assessment for learning during lessons (during independent work or plenary or whenever they check for understanding throughout the lesson).
From September 2026, students in Years 7–10 complete two formal interim assessments each academic year. Students in Years 11–13 complete three formal interim assessments to support public examination preparation and post-16 study. For Years 10 and11, we expect students to demonstrate their understanding of complex composite knowledge as reflected in GCSE style questions. For Years 12 and 13 students will demonstrate understanding directly linked either to A level specifications or to the BTEC externally examined units and learning aims.
Students and parents receive real time assessment judgements on the extent of student learning through DPR. These judgments tend to change regularly and therefore we encourage parents to login to DPR frequently and have conversations with their child about their progress. During parents’ evening, we provide the child’s DPR in printed form, which reflects the progress made by students at that specific time. Teachers may also use DPR Collaborations to provide personalised feedback and targeted next steps, enabling students to revisit misconceptions and secure key objectives.

10. At Key Stage 5,challenging targets are set based on a student’s Key Stage 4 outcomes using ALPS. Students who meet their ALPS attainment targets at the end of Key Stage 5 would be achieving above or in line with national averages.
2.4. How we provide careers information, advice and guidance to our students
Our Careers and Aspirations Manager runs a drop-in session as well as face-to-face interviews for all students about their career needs.
All of our KS4 and KS5 students receive a face-to-face impartial careers information and guidance interview with an external Careers Advisor from Future Smart Careers (at the end of Year 10, in Year 12 and again in Year 13.
We organise a week’s work experience for our Year 10 and Year 12 students. Students take part in a Careers Fair organised by our Careers and Aspirations Manager ..
The Careers Hub works closely with employers, higher education providers and training organisations to promote meaningful encounters with the world of work through visits, speakers, workshops and enrichment opportunities.
We have a clear programme of studies to support our students to successfully attend our sixth form and gain access to Russell Group Universities and high quality apprenticeships when they leave year 13.
We work closely with parents, employers, higher education providers and training organisations to ensure students are well informed about their future education, training and career pathways.

Exam Results
KS5 Results
Sixth Form Results 2026
Strong progress for Haggerston Sixth Form students
Haggerston Sixth Form students are also celebrating strong results in 2026.
Academic outcomes improved significantly, with value added rising from -0.19 to +0.12, meaning students studying academic qualifications made substantially stronger progress from their starting points.
Students secured places at a wide range of universities and progressed to further study, apprenticeships and employment.
Alongside their main qualifications, students also embraced opportunities to extend themselves academically through the Extended Project Qualification (EPQ) and Higher Project Qualification (HPQ).
We are delighted with the progress made and remain focused on ensuring that every Haggerston Sixth Form student leaves us with excellent qualifications and ambitious destinations.
KS4 Results
GCSE Results 2026
Haggerston students celebrate excellent GCSE results
Students and staff at Haggerston School are celebrating an excellent set of GCSE results, with outcomes improving significantly across a number of key measures.
These results reflect the hard work and ambition of our students and the commitment of staff across the school. We are particularly pleased to see stronger outcomes for disadvantaged students and a significant rise in the proportion of students securing strong passes in both English and Mathematics.
Executive Headteacher Thahmina Begum said:
“We are incredibly proud of our Year 11 students. These results represent a significant improvement for Haggerston and, most importantly, reflect the hard work of our young people and the staff who have supported them.
We are ambitious for every student at Haggerston. While there is much to celebrate, we will continue to build on these results, particularly by securing even more of the highest grades and ensuring that every student, regardless of background, achieves exceptionally well.”
